Finance and Investments

This text combines investments (present value, bonds, the term structure, stock valuation, portfolio theory, the CAPM, efficient markets) with financial economics (expected utility, consumption-based asset pricing, no-arbitrage, options and futures, corporate debt and capital structure) into one reading. The two subjects are really about the same thing from different angles:

  • investments works bottom-up: given cash flows and interest rates, how are bonds and stocks priced, and how is risk diversified in a portfolio?
  • financial economics works top-down: why do individuals price this way, and what is the general principle behind it?

The text is organised around the four elements of finance — time, risk, options and information:

Element Question Chapters
time how are resources allocated across dates? present value, bonds, term structure (1–4)
risk how are resources allocated across states? portfolios, CAPM, expected utility, SDF (6–8, 10–12)
options what is a choice worth? options, futures, corporate debt (13–15)
information do prices already contain all information? efficient markets (9)

One formula runs through everything: price = expectation of (stochastic discount factor × future payoff). The present-value formula, the CAPM, risk-neutral pricing and option pricing can all be seen as special cases under different assumptions. Each chapter first says what question it answers and the intuition, then gives formulas and derivations, and finally works the simplest numerical examples.

Prerequisites: calculus, basic probability and statistics (expectation, variance, covariance) and a little linear algebra.

Contents

  1. Overview: What Finance Studies
  2. The Time Value of Money
  3. Bonds and Yields
  4. The Term Structure of Interest Rates
  5. Duration, Convexity and Immunisation
  6. Stock Valuation

  14. Options
  15. Forwards, Futures and Swaps
  16. Corporate Debt and the Option View
  17. Capital Structure
  18. Review: One Thread

Notation

Symbol Meaning
PV,\ FV present value, future value
r,\ r_f interest rate; risk-free rate; R=1+r the gross return
y,\ s(n),\ f_{t,t+n} yield to maturity; n-period spot rate; forward rate
u(\cdot),\ \rho,\ A(x) utility; risk premium; Arrow–Pratt absolute risk aversion
m stochastic discount factor (SDF); p=E[mx]
\beta,\ \sigma,\ \rho_{ij} beta; standard deviation; correlation
C,\ P,\ S,\ X call value; put value; underlying price; strike
q,\ \pi^* risk-neutral probability
V,\ D,\ E,\ t_c firm value; debt; equity; corporate tax rate

0. Overview: What Finance Studies

Finance studies how people use markets to reallocate resources across time and across states. Without financial markets a retiree could not carry youthful income into old age; without insurance and derivatives risk would have to be borne by each person alone. A comparison of households in China and the US shows how differently intertemporal allocation can be done: US households owe about 136% of annual income and save about 3%; Chinese households owe about 17% and save 25%–50%.

Risk sharing has a long history: Chinese and Babylonian traders shared transport risk around 2000 BC, and the earliest known insurance contract dates from Genoa in 1347. Financial contracts bring two classical problems: adverse selection (hidden information) and moral hazard (hidden action).

The toolbox has three layers:

  1. a certain world: present value, bonds, term structure — only interest rates are needed;
  2. an uncertain world: portfolios, CAPM — risk is described by mean and variance;
  3. general principles: expected utility, the stochastic discount factor, no-arbitrage — a unified answer to how risk is priced, of which derivatives and corporate finance are applications.

1. The Time Value of Money

Intuition. A dollar today is worth more than a dollar next year because today's dollar can earn interest. The basis of all financial analysis is to convert cash flows at different dates to a common date before comparing them.

1.1 Present and future value

With interest rate r,

FV_T=CF_0(1+r)^T,\qquad PV_0=\frac{CF_T}{(1+r)^T}.

Example: at 12%, would you rather have 10,000 now or 11,424 a year from now? The first is worth 10000\times1.12=11200<11424 in a year. If you need money now you can borrow 11424/1.12=10200 and repay it with the 11,424 — so 11,424 next year has present value 10,200 and is better. We discount because of opportunity cost: funds always have alternative uses (bank deposits, government bonds).

Simple versus compound interest: interest can be reinvested only under compounding. 10,000 for two years: simple 12,400, compound 12,544. In well-functioning markets nothing prevents earning compound interest, so we always assume it.

1.2 Compounding frequency and the effective annual rate

A stated annual rate (APR) is meaningful only with a compounding frequency. Compounding n times a year gives the effective annual rate

\text{EAIR}=\Big(1+\frac{\text{SAIR}}n\Big)^n-1.

A stated 12%: semi-annual 12.36%, quarterly 12.55%, monthly 12.68%, approaching the continuous e^{0.12}-1. Effective rates cannot simply be divided: an effective annual 12.55% corresponds to an effective semi-annual rate of 1.03^2-1=6.09\%, not 6.28%. With continuous compounding FV=CF_0e^{rT} and the discount factor is e^{-rT}.

1.3 Annuities and perpetuities

An annuity pays a fixed C for T periods (first payment at the end of period 1):

PV=C\cdot\frac1r\Big[1-\frac1{(1+r)^T}\Big].

A perpetuity (consol): PV=C/r. Example: at 10%, 100 a year forever is worth 100/0.1=1000 — not infinite, because far-off cash flows have present value tending to zero. A growing annuity (growth g per period):

PV=\frac{C}{r-g}\Big[1-\Big(\frac{1+g}{1+r}\Big)^T\Big],\quad\text{perpetual: }PV=\frac C{r-g}\ (r>g).

1.4 Steps for using the formulas

  1. find the interest rate matching the compounding period (for monthly use APR/12);
  2. put the payments on a timeline; re-index delayed or irregular ones;
  3. sum with the formulas;
  4. the formulas assume the first payment at the end of period 1, so discount further for every period of delay;
  5. write "present value of payments = amount borrowed" and solve.

Example (mortgage): a 2 million home, a 30-year mortgage at APR 6% (monthly 0.5%), a 20,000 down payment one month from now, the first monthly payment four months from now: 163.82\,C=2{,}000{,}000-20{,}000/1.005.

Two repayment schedules: equal payments (level payment each month) and equal principal (equal principal repayments, declining interest); their present values are the same — a common feature of any fair loan.

1.5 Common mistakes

  • cash flows at different dates cannot be added directly: two years of salary 12 + 14 million is not a present value;
  • a discount loan (interest deducted up front) has an effective rate above the stated one: borrowing 10,000 at 10% with 1,000 deducted gives 9,000 and requires repaying 10,000, an effective rate of 10000/9000-1=11.1\%;
  • a perpetuity is not "worth infinity".

2. Bonds and Yields

Intuition. A bond is a string of promised cash flows. Its price is the present value of that string; its yield is the interest rate that "undoes" the price into the cash flows. Prices and rates move in opposite directions.

2.1 Terminology

Coupon, face value, maturity, coupon rate = coupon / face value. A pure-discount (zero-coupon) bond pays only the face value at maturity, is issued below face value, and its interest is implicit in the difference; a level-coupon bond pays coupons periodically and the face value at maturity; a consol has no maturity.

2.2 Price = present value of cash flows

P=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{C}{(1+r)^t}+\frac{F}{(1+r)^T}.

Example: a two-year bond, 10% coupon paid semi-annually, face value 100. At a 5% semi-annual rate the price is 100 (par); if the rate falls to 4% semi-annual the price rises to 103.63. Price and rate move oppositely: it sells at a premium when coupon rate > discount rate, at a discount when <, at par when =. Bonds are usually issued at par; if rates later rise the price falls. Flight to safety: at the start of a downturn investors sell risky assets and buy government bonds, bidding up bond prices and lowering rates.

2.3 Yield to maturity (YTM)

Given the price, find the discount rate solving P=\sum C/(1+y)^t+F/(1+y)^T. Example: the 10%-coupon two-year bond at a price of 103.63 has a semi-annual YTM of 4%; a bond priced at 900 has a YTM of 16.25% (Excel: IRR). YTM is usually quoted annually; the effective annual yield is (1+y/2)^2-1; the current yield = current coupon / price. YTM is the average return from holding to maturity, but assumes coupons are reinvested at the YTM.

2.4 Nominal and real rates

1+\text{nominal}=(1+\text{real})(1+\text{inflation})\ \Rightarrow\ \text{nominal}\approx\text{real}+\text{inflation}\ \text{(Fisher)}.

Example: nominal 2.04%, inflation 6% ⟹ real -3.74\%: the deposit grows by 2.04% but purchasing power falls by 3.74%. Nominal cash flows are discounted at nominal rates, real cash flows at real rates, with the same present value — we need not adjust present values for inflation, only use the right discount rate.

2.5 Holding-period return and NPV

The holding-period return is r_{hp}=V_{end}/V_{begin}-1, with V_{end} including reinvested proceeds. Example: buy at 1150 with annual coupon 100, price 1020 after one year, sell at 1070 after two: the first coupon buys 100/1020=0.098 units, V_{end}=(1070+100)(1.098)=1284.66, a two-year holding-period return of 11.7\%, annualised about 11.1\%.

Net present value (NPV) = present value of future cash flows − cost. A price equal to the present value (NPV = 0) does not mean the investor "earns nothing" — he earns the discount rate. NPV>0 means a return above the market rate. Example: 100 received in a month for a cost of 90 with a 10% monthly rate: return 100/90-1=11.1\%>10\%, NPV>0.

The main risks of a bond: default risk (credit ratings from Aaa/AAA to C; Baa/BBB and above is investment grade, below is high-yield/junk) and inflation risk.

3. The Term Structure of Interest Rates

Intuition. The price of funds differs by maturity: borrowing for one year and for ten years carry different rates. The yield curve plots this difference; it is both the basis of pricing (cash flows at different dates are discounted at different rates) and a forecast of the future.

3.1 Short rates, spot rates and yields

The short rate r_t is the rate for borrowing in period t. The yield of a zero-coupon bond is the geometric average of short rates:

1+y(n)=\big[(1+r_1)(1+r_2)\cdots(1+r_n)\big]^{1/n}.

The spot rate s(n) is today's annualised rate for an investment of n periods, equal to the yield of an n-period zero. Example: short rates (8\%,10\%,11\%,11\%): s(2)=9.0\%, s(3)=9.66\%, s(4)=9.99\%. If short rates rise, so does s(n) — a spot rate is an average of short rates.

Present value under a non-flat curve: discount each cash flow at its own spot rate, PV=\sum CF_t/(1+s(t))^t.

3.2 Stripping coupon bonds and extracting spot rates

Any coupon bond can be decomposed into zero-coupon bonds. Example: a three-year, 8% annual-coupon bond with face value 1000 = zeros with face values 80 (1 year), 80 (2 years), 1080 (3 years), priced at the corresponding spot rates. Conversely, with only short zeros available, longer spot rates can be recursively backed out from coupon-bond prices; two coupon bonds can also be combined into a zero (short 0.8 of a 10% coupon bond and buy 1 of an 8% coupon bond: a zero paying 200 in year 10).

3.3 Forward rates

The forward rate f_{t_1,t_2} is the rate, agreed today, for borrowing between future dates t_1 and t_2, implied by spot rates:

(1+s(t_2))^{t_2}=(1+s(t_1))^{t_1}(1+f_{t_1,t_2})^{t_2-t_1}.

Example: s(2)=8.995\%,\ s(3)=9.66\% ⟹ f_{2,3}=1.0966^3/1.08995^2-1=11\%. Also (1+f_{t,t+n})^n=(1+f_{t,t+1})\cdots(1+f_{t+n-1,t+n}).

A synthetic forward loan: using a 1-year zero (price 925.93, y(1)=8\%) and a 2-year zero one can lock in "borrow 1000 at the end of year 1, repay 1050 at the end of year 2" (forward rate 5%): short 1.05 units of the 2-year zero and buy the 1-year zero — zero cash flow today.

Example: a three-year 6% annual coupon bond priced at 1030, a one-year zero at 985.22 and a two-year zero at 961.17 (face 1000): YTM y=4.90\%; s(1)=1.5\%, s(2)=2.5\%, s(3)=5.09\% (the YTM differs from every spot rate — the YTM is the average return of the coupon bond, s(3) that of a three-year zero); f_{1,3}=6.93\%.

3.4 Theories of the term structure

Without uncertainty f_{t,t+1}=r_{t+1}. Under uncertainty:

  • Expectations theory: the forward rate equals the market's expectation of the future short rate, f_{1,2}=E[r_2]. An upward-sloping curve = rates expected to rise (expected inflation or tightening); an inverted curve = rates expected to fall. But upward-sloping curves are far more common than inverted ones in the data — if rises and falls were equally likely the two would be equally common.
  • Liquidity preference: most investors prefer short bonds (long bonds are more sensitive to rates and riskier), so long bonds must carry a liquidity premium LP=f_{n,n+1}-E[r_{n+1}]>0: f_{n,n+1}=E[r_{n+1}]+LP. (Here "liquidity" means preference for short maturities, not ease of trading.)

Curve shapes can then be read: slowly rising (LP and expected short rates constant, or expected rates falling while LP rises faster); steeply rising (LP and expected rates both rising, common early in an expansion); flat (expected rates unchanged and LP\approx0, often at turning points); hump-shaped (expected short rates falling with constant LP); inverted (expected short rates falling) — usually a sign of slowdown, and the shape is used to forecast recessions 2–6 quarters ahead. Caution: expected rate rises make the curve slope upward, but an upward slope does not necessarily mean rates are expected to rise (it may be just LP).

4. Duration, Convexity and Immunisation

Intuition. When rates change, how much does a bond's price move? Long bonds move more; and a coupon bond moves less than a zero of the same maturity because its cash flows "on average" arrive earlier — duration is this "effective maturity".

4.1 Duration

Example: for an 8% coupon bond, YTM rising from 8% to 9%, price changes grow with maturity at 1, 10, 20 years; zeros move more than coupon bonds of the same maturity. Macaulay duration is the weighted average of the times to the cash flows, with weights the share of each payment's present value in the bond price:

D=\sum_t t\cdot\frac{PV(CF_t)}{P}.

The duration of a zero equals its maturity. For an annual-coupon bond at par D=\dfrac{1+y}{y}\Big[1-\dfrac1{(1+y)^T}\Big]. The modified duration D^*=D/(1+y) satisfies

\frac{\Delta P}{P}\approx-D^*\,\Delta y.

Example: a 30-year 8% bond at y=8\%: D=12.16, D^*=11.26 — a one-percentage-point rise in yield cuts the price by about 11.26%. Properties: lower coupon, longer maturity and lower yield all lengthen duration.

4.2 Convexity

Duration is only the tangent (first-order approximation) of the price–yield curve; it is accurate for small changes only: the curve is convex, so when rates fall the true gain exceeds the tangent's prediction and when rates rise the loss is smaller. Convexity is the second-order term,

\frac{\Delta P}{P}\approx-D^*\Delta y+\tfrac12\,\text{Convexity}\,(\Delta y)^2.

Convexity is desirable: at equal duration a more convex bond rises more and falls less.

4.3 Immunisation

Bank assets (loans, mortgages) have long duration and liabilities (deposits) short duration; an unexpected rate rise cuts assets more than liabilities and hurts net worth. Pension funds and insurers with fixed future obligations face the same mismatch. Immunisation: match the duration of assets to that of liabilities.

Example: an insurer issues a 5-year guaranteed investment contract: 10000\times1.08^5=14693.28. Funding it with a 6-year zero (duration 6), a rate rise to 10% leaves proceeds of 14,426.13, a shortfall of 267.15. Investing 10,000 in a coupon bond with duration 5 (6-year, 8% annual coupon, D=(1.08/0.08)(1-1/1.08^6)=4.99) with coupons reinvested gives a year-5 value nearly equal to the obligation, for rate rises and falls alike. Portfolio duration is the weighted average of component durations.

Example: a pension fund must pay 19,487 in 7 years (present value 10,000 at 10%, duration 7). Immunise with a 3-year zero (duration 3) and a consol (duration 1.1/0.1=11): 3x+11(1-x)=7 ⟹ x=1/2, 5,000 each. One year later the liability's duration is 6, so rebalance: the zero has duration 2, the consol still 11, x=5/9, so hold 11000\times5/9=6111.11 in zeros and 4888.89 in consols. Immunisation is dynamic and needs rebalancing.

5. Stock Valuation

Intuition. A stock's price is the present value of its future dividends. How a firm decides how much to retain and how much to pay out determines how dividends grow, and hence the price.

5.1 Basics of stocks

Common stock (voting rights, residual claim, limited liability), preferred stock (fixed dividend, priority claim; cumulative, convertible, callable). Issuance: IPOs and seasoned offerings. Dividends: cash dividends, stock dividends, splits (after a 3:1 split the price per share is 1/3 and shares outstanding triple), repurchases (another way of returning cash to shareholders). On the ex-dividend date the price falls by about the dividend.

5.2 The dividend discount model (DDM)

Holding for one year: P_0=\dfrac{D_1+P_1}{1+r}. Substituting repeatedly and excluding bubbles (\lim P_T/(1+r)^T=0):

P_0=\sum_{t=1}^\infty\frac{D_t}{(1+r)^t}.

Even a firm that lives forever and pays no dividends for years has a positive price — because the market expects it to pay dividends eventually. With dividends growing at a constant rate g (the Gordon model):

P_0=\frac{D_1}{r-g}\qquad(r>g),\qquad r=\frac{D_1}{P_0}+g,

i.e. required return = dividend yield + capital-gain yield.

5.3 Growth comes from reinvestment

Suppose earnings E stay constant unless new investment is made and financing comes only from retained earnings. With payout ratio \delta=D/E, retention ratio 1-\delta and return R on new investment:

g=(1-\delta)R.

Example: earnings per share 5, from period 1 retain 40% and invest at 20% in perpetuity, discount rate 12%. Earnings grow at g=0.4\times0.2=8\% (E_2=5+0.4=5.4) and dividends are 60% of earnings, so P=D_1/(r-g)=3/(0.12-0.08)=75.

5.4 The NPVGO model

P=\frac Er+\text{NPVGO}

price = value of assets in place (the perpetuity of fully distributed earnings) + net present value of growth opportunities. New investment adds value only if R>r: when R=r dividend policy does not matter; when R>r retain everything; when R<r pay everything out.

Example: a one-off investment (retain 40% at a quarterly R=20\%, discount rate 12%): without investment P=5/0.12=41.67; NPVGO =(-2+0.4/0.12)/1.12=1.19, P'=42.86; larger retention gives larger NPVGO (50%: 1.49; 60%: 1.79; 70%: 2.08; 100%: 2.98, P'=44.65). If the investment recurs every period, P=5/0.12+1.3333/(0.12-0.08)=75. With 100% retention g=R=20\%>r and the price formula breaks down — in reality good opportunities do not repeat forever and R falls as demand for them rises. Growth is not the same as value: with R=10\%<r=12\%, g=4\%>0 but P'=41.67-4.17=37.50 — NPVGO is negative.

5.5 The price–earnings ratio

\dfrac PE=\dfrac1r+\dfrac{\text{NPVGO}}E: firms with abundant growth opportunities have high P/E (high-tech and emerging firms; Starbucks' P/E was 50 in 2006 and 19 in 2008); mature firms have low P/E (Ford 7.69). P/E is like a house's price–rent ratio. Limitations: EPS is an accounting number that can be manipulated; there is no absolute level that tells whether any stock is cheap or dear.

5.6 Multi-stage growth

Dividend growth varies for the first T years and is constant afterwards. Example: dividend just paid 5.25, growth 14% next year falling by 3 percentage points a year until the industry's 5%, which is maintained forever, required return 14%: the price is 71.70. The Gordon model's main weakness is that it takes the discount rate r as exogenous — a complete asset-pricing model must say what determines r (Chapters 8 and 11).

6. Statistical Description of Returns

Intuition. Admitting that the future is random means discounting expected payoffs, with a discount rate that allows for risk. This chapter collects the statistics needed.

A random variable is a function on a probability space, described by its distribution; a constant is a special case.

  • expectation E[X]=\sum p_sx_s (probability-weighted average);
  • variance \mathrm{Var}(X)=E[(X-EX)^2], standard deviation \sigma=\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}} (same units as returns, a common risk measure);
  • covariance \mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=E[(X-EX)(Y-EY)], with variance the special case \mathrm{Cov}(X,X);
  • correlation \rho=\mathrm{Cov}/(\sigma_X\sigma_Y)\in[-1,1] = expected product of the standardised variables.

Example (Supertech and Slowpoke), four equally likely states: Supertech returns (-20,10,30,50)\%, E=17.5\%, variance 668.75\times10^{-4}; Slowpoke (5,20,-12,9)\%, E=5.5\%, variance 132.25\times10^{-4}; covariance -48.75\times10^{-4}, correlation -0.16.

Properties: \rho(a+bX,Y)=\pm\rho(X,Y) (sign of b); the best linear predictor minimising E[(Y-a-bX)^2] has b=\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)/\mathrm{Var}(X), a=E[Y]-bE[X] and minimum mean squared error \mathrm{Var}(Y)(1-\rho^2); \rho=\pm1 iff Y=a+bX (b\gtrless0). The correlation between two two-state random variables is always \pm1 (for 0<p<1). Gamble example: X=(2,-1), Y=(5,-5): \rho=1 for any p; for Y=(-5,5), \rho=-1.

7. Portfolio Theory

Intuition. Don't put all your eggs in one basket. A portfolio's expected return is the weighted average of those of its assets, but its risk is not — when assets are imperfectly correlated the portfolio's risk is below the weighted average: this is diversification.

7.1 Portfolio weights and short selling

A portfolio weight w_i is the share of wealth invested in asset i; weights sum to 1, may be negative and may exceed 1. Example: with 1000 and 1100 put in IBM, w_{IBM}=110\%,\ w_{GM}=-10\%; a negative weight means borrowing (shorting). Short selling: selling a security you do not own (borrowed from a broker) and buying it back later; profitable if the price is expected to fall; requires a margin account and the short seller owes any dividends to the lender. Example: GM at 10; Alan borrows and sells 10 shares for 100; when the price falls to 6 he buys back for 60 and returns the shares, keeping 40.

7.2 Two assets

E[r_p]=w_1E[r_1]+(1-w_1)E[r_2],
\sigma_p^2=w_1^2\sigma_1^2+w_2^2\sigma_2^2+2w_1w_2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2.

Example: 300 in IBM (E=8.33\%,\ \sigma=25\%) and 700 in GM (E=0.715\%,\ \sigma=3.58\%), \mathrm{Cov}=8.9375\times10^{-3}: E[r_p]=3.0\%. If GM's payoffs are reversed, means and standard deviations are unchanged but \rho=-1 and portfolio variance drops sharply — negative covariance reduces risk.

Portfolio curves for different correlations: for \rho=1 a straight line between the two points; for \rho=-1 a zero-risk portfolio exists; for -1<\rho<1 a curve bowing to the left — always less risk than the straight line, which is diversification.

7.3 Many assets and the mean–variance frontier

For n assets \sigma_p^2=\sum_i\sum_jw_iw_j\sigma_{ij}: n variance terms and n^2-n covariance terms. With equal weights, all variances \sigma^2 and all covariances cov:

\sigma_p^2=\frac{\sigma^2}n+\Big(1-\frac1n\Big)\text{cov}.

More assets eliminate idiosyncratic risk (the variance term) but cannot get below systematic risk (the covariance term). A security's risk contribution is measured by covariance: a very volatile security may contribute nothing to portfolio risk.

The mean–variance frontier: for a given expected return m, minimise \frac12\sum\sum w_iw_j\sigma_{ij} subject to \sum w_i=1, \sum w_iE[r_i]=m; the Lagrangian gives n+2 linear equations; the minimum variance is a quadratic in m, so the frontier is a hyperbola in the \sigma–E plane. Example: three uncorrelated securities with variance 1 and expected returns 1, 2, 3: w_1=\frac43-\frac m2,\ w_2=\frac13,\ w_3=\frac m2-\frac23, \mathrm{Var}(r_p)=m^2-2m+\frac73.

Definitions: the feasible (opportunity) set is all attainable portfolios; the mean–variance frontier is the minimum-variance portfolios for each expected return; the efficient frontier is its upper part (maximum expected return for given risk); the minimum-variance portfolio is its leftmost point.

8. The Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM)

Intuition. If everyone invests in a mean–variance optimal way and agrees about the market, then everyone's portfolio of risky assets is necessarily the same — the market portfolio. A security's risk is determined only by its contribution to the market portfolio's risk (its covariance, i.e. \beta).

8.1 Adding a risk-free asset

Mixing the risk-free asset with a risky portfolio A: E(r_P)=r_f+\dfrac{E(r_A)-r_f}{\sigma_A}\,\sigma_P, a straight line. Connecting the risk-free point to the frontier, the steepest line is tangent to the hyperbola at the tangency portfolio, and the efficient frontier becomes this straight line.

8.2 Two-fund separation

Every optimal portfolio is a mix of the tangency portfolio and the risk-free asset: very risk-averse investors hold more of the riskless asset, tolerant ones more of the tangency portfolio, even borrowing. Whatever the risk attitude, everyone chooses the same risky portfolio.

When is mean–variance the right criterion? When investors like high mean and low variance: quadratic utility u(c)=-(c-\bar c)^2 (E[u] depends only on mean and variance), or all returns jointly normal.

8.3 The market portfolio and the capital market line

Assume mean–variance preferences, homogeneous expectations and perfect markets. Everyone holds the same risky portfolio ⟹ it must be the market portfolio (all risky securities, weights = market values): every security has a positive weight (otherwise nobody would hold it and its price would fall until someone would); its composition does not depend on preferences.

The capital market line (CML): the relation between expected return and risk for efficient portfolios,

E(r_e)=r_f+\frac{E(r_m)-r_f}{\sigma_m}\,\sigma_e,

whose slope (the market's Sharpe ratio) is the price of risk: the expected return the market pays for each extra unit of standard deviation.

8.4 The security market line

A security's contribution to the market portfolio's variance is its covariance with the market \sigma_{im}=\mathrm{Cov}(r_i,r_m) (since \mathrm{Var}(r_m)=\sum_iw_{mi}\sigma_{im}). Standardising gives beta

\beta_i=\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(r_i,r_m)}{\mathrm{Var}(r_m)}=\rho_{im}\frac{\sigma_i}{\sigma_m},

and a portfolio's \beta is the weighted average of its assets' betas.

CAPM: E(r_i)=r_f+\beta_i\,[E(r_m)-r_f]

On the security market line (SML) the expected risk premium is proportional to \beta with the market premium as the factor of proportionality. In equilibrium only systematic risk (the part correlated with the market) is compensated; idiosyncratic risk can be diversified away and is not priced.

8.5 Assessing the CAPM

  • do investors actually hold diversified portfolios? The largest mutual funds are index funds and institutions hold much stock — but many individuals are under-diversified;
  • human capital should count too: an employee's income is positively correlated with her company's stock, so in theory she should short it — in practice almost nobody does; many people bet on hunches, holding a few familiar stocks, contrary to the assumption that nobody has valuable information;
  • empirically: the CAPM predicts that higher-\beta stocks have higher average returns (average returns lie on the SML); in the data the relation is weak or absent;
  • but even if the CAPM is not descriptively accurate it remains valuable as a normative tool (how to decide, how to estimate the cost of capital).

9. Efficient Markets

Intuition. If prices already reflect all information, one cannot earn excess returns from that information alone. Prices react only to surprises.

9.1 Definition and examples

A market is efficient with respect to an information set iff that information is fully reflected in prices; in an efficient market you cannot earn more than the normal return unless you have information beyond what is in prices.

Example (Lenovo): dividends cycle 1,2,1,2,\dots, discount rate 10%, risk-neutral. The price alternates between 14.76 and 15.24 and the return each year is 10% — the cyclicality is fully reflected and cannot be exploited; the market is efficient with respect to it. If instead investors remember only the current dividend and assume it is permanent, the price would be 10,20,10,20,\dots — someone who knows of the cycle buys at 10 when the dividend is 1 and sells at 20 next period (return 110%), and shorts at 20 when the dividend is 2 — the market is inefficient with respect to that information.

Prices react only to surprises: in July 2012 Apple reported $8.8 billion quarterly profit and its share price still fell about 5%, because investors expected even more; when China's central bank raised the rate by 0.25% in April the Shanghai index rose next day — the hike was smaller than feared. Implication for investing: the relevant information is that not already in prices; if you do not believe you have such information, you should conclude assets are fairly priced.

9.2 Three forms of efficiency

  • weak form: prices reflect past prices and trading data ⟹ technical analysis is useless;
  • semi-strong form: prices reflect all public information ⟹ fundamental analysis is useless too;
  • strong form: prices reflect all information, including inside information ⟹ insider trading is useless.

Strong ⟹ semi-strong ⟹ weak. Technical analysis trades on price patterns (resistance and support levels); fundamental analysis estimates earnings, dividends, rates and risk, presuming prices fluctuate around fundamental value. Note that in an efficient market price equals fundamental value rather than fluctuating around it. Insider trading is banned by the SEC (the Martha Stewart case; in China the Huang Guangyu case).

9.3 Empirical evidence

Weak form: efficiency implies prices follow a random walk P_{t+1}=P_t+\text{expected return}+\text{random error} with zero serial correlation. Studies find positive correlation at short and intermediate horizons (momentum) and negative at long horizons, but the coefficients are small relative to estimation error — statistical significance is not economic significance and no reliable profitable strategy follows. Semi-strong form: mutual funds on average do not beat the market; in event studies the abnormal return AR_t=r_t-(a+br_{Mt}) and the cumulative abnormal return (CAR) show good news fully incorporated on the announcement date with no further drift — most studies support semi-strong efficiency.

Evidence against: on 19 October 1987 the NYSE fell almost 25% in a day with no obvious news; post-earnings-announcement drift. The Grossman–Stiglitz paradox: if markets are inefficient investors search for mispricings and trade them away; if markets are efficient nobody bothers to search — so the market becomes inefficient again. Conclusion: pricing anomalies can appear and persist for a while but not forever; efficiency is a long-run tendency — "if any $100 bills are lying around the stock exchanges of the world, they will not be there for long."

10. Expected Utility and Risk Aversion

Intuition. So far we described preferences by mean and variance. More fundamentally, preferences are defined over lotteries (probability distributions) and represented by expected utility. Risk aversion = a concave utility function.

10.1 Expected utility and risk aversion

Without uncertainty preferences are represented by a utility function (preferences must be "complete and transitive" to be rational). With uncertainty the objects of preference are lotteries and expected utility is U=E[u(c)]=\sum p_su(c_s) (von Neumann–Morgenstern utility; u state-independent if it does not depend on the state; needs continuity, the independence axiom, etc.).

Risk aversion: for any wealth y and random gamble z, u(y+E[z])\ge E[u(y+z)] (one prefers the expected value of a gamble to the gamble itself). Risk aversion ⟺ u concave (u''\le0); risk neutrality ⟺ u linear.

The certainty equivalent C(y,z): E[u(y+z)]=u(y+C). The risk premium \rho(y,z): the most one would pay out of E[z] to avoid the gamble, E[u(y+z)]=u(y+E[z]-\rho), so C=E[z]-\rho. Risk aversion ⟺ \rho\ge0. Property: \rho(y,z)=\rho(y+E[z],z-E[z]) — only zero-mean gambles need considering.

Example 1: y=5, z=\pm3 with equal odds. For u=\ln x: \tfrac12\ln2+\tfrac12\ln8=\ln(5-\rho) ⟹ \rho=1, C=4 (that is -1 relative to E[z]=0); u=-1/\ln x is more risk averse, with \rho=2.17. Example 2: u(x)=-e^{-ax}, \rho(y,z)=E[z]+\ln E[e^{-az}]/a; if z is normal then \rho=a\mathrm{Var}(z)/2, independent of y.

10.2 Arrow–Pratt measures

A(x)=-\frac{u''(x)}{u'(x)}\ (\text{absolute risk aversion}),\quad T(x)=\frac1{A(x)}\ (\text{risk tolerance}),\quad R(x)=xA(x)\ (\text{relative risk aversion}).

Dividing by u' makes the measure invariant to affine transformations of u; it is the curvature of u.

Pratt's theorem. For strictly increasing, twice continuously differentiable u_1,u_2 the following are equivalent: (i) A_1(y)\ge A_2(y) for all y; (ii) \rho_1(y,z)\ge\rho_2(y,z) for all y,z; (iii) u_1 is a concave transformation of u_2: u_1=f\circ u_2, f concave.

Proof sketch: (i)⟹(iii) let f(t)=u_1(u_2^{-1}(t)); f'>0 and f''=[A_2(y)-A_1(y)]u_1'(y)/(u_2'(y))^2\le0; (iii)⟹(ii) Jensen: E[u_1(y+z)]=E[f(u_2(y+z))]\le f(E[u_2]); (ii)⟹(i) by contradiction. Example: u_i=-e^{-a_iy}, a_1\ge a_2, \rho_i=a_i\mathrm{Var}(z)/2.

Common classes: CARA (A'=0, u=-e^{-ax}); IARA (A'>0, e.g. quadratic); DARA (A'<0) — empirical evidence favours DARA. CRRA (R'=0) implies DARA (R'=A+xA'=0 and x,A>0 ⟹ A'<0) and has nice mathematics: u=\dfrac{x^{1-a}}{1-a}, log utility at a=1; they belong to the HARA (linear risk tolerance) family.

How large is a? Wealth W is doubled with probability p or halved with probability 1-p; pick p to be indifferent: p=0.5\Rightarrow a=1; p=0.667\Rightarrow a=2; p=0.8\Rightarrow a=3; p=0.9\Rightarrow a=4.2; p=0.99\Rightarrow a=7.6; p=0.9999\Rightarrow a=14.3. Most people's relative risk aversion lies in (0,6).

10.3 One risky and one riskless asset

Wealth W_0, gross risky return R, riskless R_f, amount a in the risky asset:

\max_aE[u(W_0R_f+(R-R_f)a)],\qquad\text{FOC:}\ E[u'(W)(R-R_f)]=0.

Result: a^*>0 ⟺ E[R]>R_f (the second-order condition E[u''(W)(R-R_f)^2]<0 ensures concavity). Wealth effects: DARA ⟹ the risky asset is a normal good (more wealth, more held); IARA ⟹ inferior; CARA ⟹ independent of wealth. Example: R_f=1.1, R=2 or 0.8 equally likely: log utility a=11W_0/9 (increasing in W_0); CARA (u=-e^{-x}) a=\ln3/1.2\approx0.9155 (independent of W_0); quadratic a=10c/3-11W_0/3 (decreasing). Wealth elasticity: less than 1 for IRRA, more than 1 for DRRA, equal to 1 for CRRA.

10.4 Many risky assets: two-fund separation

With several risky assets a DARA investor might reduce one risky asset and raise another as wealth grows. Two-fund monetary separation — the optimal portfolio is always a mix of the riskless asset and a fixed fund of risky assets — holds iff marginal utility has the form u'(y)=(A+By)^C or u'(y)=Ae^{By} (utility with linear risk tolerance; Cass–Stiglitz 1970).

10.5 Greater risk

What does it mean for a gamble Y to be riskier than X? Rothschild–Stiglitz: there is noise Z with E[Z|X]=0 such that Y-E[Y]\overset d=X-E[X]+Z.

Proposition: for equal means, Y is riskier than X ⟺ every risk-averse person (every concave u) prefers X ⟺ E[u(Y)]\le E[u(X)] ⟺ Y's risk premium is at least X's.

Proof of (⟹): E[u(X+Z)]=E[E[u(X+Z)|X]]\le E[u(X)] (Jensen). Greater risk ≠ greater variance: X\in\{1,3,4,6\}, Y=2 (prob. 1/2), 3, 7 (1/4 each), E=3.5, \mathrm{Var}(Y)=4.25>\mathrm{Var}(X)=3.25, yet under log utility E\ln Y=\ln84/4>E\ln X=\ln72/4. The variance ordering corresponds to quadratic utility, greater risk to all concave utilities, hence more general; exception: for normal X,Y the two coincide. A riskier gamble also has a higher risk premium (y=5: \pm4 has premium 2 > the premium 1 of \pm3).

11. Consumption-Based Asset Pricing

Intuition. Why do stocks have higher expected returns than bonds? Because stocks pay badly in bad times (low consumption, high marginal utility); such assets are risky and need extra compensation. An asset's price is determined by the covariance of its payoff with marginal utility.

11.1 The representative consumer and the Euler equation

An exchange economy: exogenous endowments, one perishable good, no money, n assets (zero net supply) with payoffs x_i (in goods). The representative consumer maximises u(c_0)+\beta E[u(c_1)] (\beta measures patience) with c_0=e_0-\sum p_ih_i, c_1=e_1+\sum h_ix_i. Differentiating in h_i gives the Euler equation

p_iu'(c_0)=\beta E[u'(c_1)x_i].

The left side is the marginal-utility loss from giving up p_i now, the right side the expected marginal-utility gain from the future payoff. Define the stochastic discount factor (SDF, pricing kernel) m=\beta u'(c_1)/u'(c_0) (the marginal rate of substitution):

p_i=E[m\,x_i]\qquad\text{(the most general asset-pricing formula)}

Different asset-pricing models just play with m.

A riskless bond (x=1): p_f=E[m], R_f=1/E[m] — where interest rates come from. Example: u=\ln c, \beta=1, c_0=1, tomorrow c_1=(3,1) (equally likely): m=c_0/c_1=(1/3,1), p_f=2/3, R_f=1.5; a stock paying x=(4,-1): p=E[mx]=1/6, expected return E[x]/p=9.

Special cases: with no uncertainty p=x/R_f (the present-value formula); risk neutrality (u linear): m=\beta, p=E[x]/R_f; in general p=E[x]/R_i (an asset-specific risk-adjusted rate), while p=E[mx] uses a single stochastic discount factor common to all assets. In multiple periods (no bubbles): p_t=E_t\sum_{k\ge1}\prod m\cdot d_{t+k} — the generalisation of the dividend discount model.

11.2 The risk correction

From the definition of covariance E[mx]=E[m]E[x]+\mathrm{Cov}(m,x):

p=\frac{E[x]}{R_f}+\mathrm{Cov}(m,x)\qquad\text{price = expected payoff discounted at the riskless rate + a risk correction}.

If the payoff is positively correlated with m (pays well when marginal utility is high — when you are "hungry") the asset is a valuable insurance: positive correction, lower expected return; if negatively correlated (pays well when you are "full") the asset is risky: lower price, higher expected return. A volatile asset is not necessarily risky: if \mathrm{Cov}(m,x)=0 the price is E[x]/R_f however large \mathrm{Var}(x) — systematic risk (the part correlated with m) is priced, idiosyncratic risk (the part uncorrelated) is not. Regressing x=bm+\varepsilon, the price depends only on bm.

In returns: 1=E[mR_i] ⟹ E[R_i]-R_f=-R_f\,\mathrm{Cov}(m,R_i). An asset positively correlated with marginal utility has a negative risk premium, a negatively correlated one a positive premium.

11.3 CRRA and log-normal consumption: determinants of the interest rate

u=c^{1-a}/(1-a), \Delta\ln c_{t+1}\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2). Using E[e^{aX}]=e^{a\mu+a^2\sigma^2/2}, the continuously compounded riskless rate is

r_f=-\ln\beta+a\mu-\tfrac12a^2\sigma^2.

Determinants: patience (more patient, lower rate), consumption growth (higher growth, higher rate), risk (higher risk, lower rate — precautionary saving), and risk aversion makes the rate more sensitive to growth.

Market clearing: in the representative-agent model there is no trade (h_i=0), c_t=e_t (Robinson Crusoe finds nobody to trade with and eats everything). Prices are supported by the requirement that the Euler equation hold — if it did not he would want to trade and the market would not clear. Note that these models address only the demand side; supply is reduced to an exogenous endowment process.

Example: log utility, \beta=1, endowment 1 today and 1 (bad) or 3 (good) tomorrow, equally likely. m=(1,1/3), p_f=2/3. Stock U pays (0,2): p_U=1/3, R_U=3; stock V pays (2,0): p_V=1, R_V=1. U pays in the good state, when you need it least, so it is risky with risk correction -1/3; V pays in the bad state with correction +1/3.

11.4 Lucas's tree and the equity premium puzzle

The stock index is a claim on the economy's whole output, dividends =e_t=c_t (Lucas's tree). With i.i.d. log-normal consumption the price–dividend ratio is constant and the gap between the expected return on equity and the riskless rate is approximately

E[r_e]-r_f\approx a\,\sigma^2\quad(\text{relative risk aversion}\times\text{variance of consumption growth}).

Data: the historical average real equity return is about 6%, the real 3-month T-bill rate about 1%, so the equity premium is about 5%; consumption growth \mu\approx2\%, \sigma\approx3\%, patience \beta\approx0.98, a\in(0,6). Result: only an absurdly high risk aversion produces a large enough premium — for reasonable a the premium is a fraction of a percentage point. This is the equity premium puzzle.

The Hansen–Jagannathan bound: \mathrm{Corr}(m,R_i)\in[-1,1] gives

\frac{|E[R_i]-R_f|}{\sigma(R_i)}\le\frac{\sigma(m)}{E[m]}.

The left side is the Sharpe ratio. US stocks have a high Sharpe ratio while consumption growth is very smooth, so making \sigma(m) big enough needs a\approx45. The essential problem: consumption data do not vary enough to justify so large a premium.

Possible directions: improve expected utility (the Allais paradox violates the independence axiom: choosing A=(0,1,0) over B=(.01,.89,.10) while choosing B'=(.90,0,.10) over A'=(.89,.11,0) contradicts expected utility); fix the consumption data; heterogeneous consumers (trade appears); incomplete markets; imperfect information and learning; rare disasters.

11.5 The beta representation and the frontier

From E[R_i]-R_f=-R_f\mathrm{Cov}(m,R_i)=\beta_{i,-m}\lambda_m with \beta_{i,-m}=\mathrm{Cov}(R_i,-m)/\mathrm{Var}(m) and \lambda_m=\mathrm{Var}(m)/E[m] (the price of risk) we get the single-beta pricing model, more general than the CAPM (which takes the market portfolio's return as a linear function of m). In the example above \lambda=1/6, \beta_U=9,\ \beta_V=-3. The Sharpe ratio is largest when an asset's return is perfectly negatively correlated with m, equal to \sigma(m)/E[m] (the HJ bound) — all returns on the mean–variance efficient frontier are perfectly negatively correlated with m and hence with each other, and m=a+bR_{mv}. Any mean–variance efficient return contains all the information needed for pricing; the CAPM is the special case in which the market portfolio lies on the efficient frontier.

12. Complete Markets, No Arbitrage and Risk-Neutral Pricing

Intuition. The last chapter derived p=E[mx] from equilibrium. Can we drop equilibrium and use only "no free lunch"? Yes: no arbitrage alone guarantees a positive SDF.

12.1 Security markets and complete markets

There are S future states and J securities with payoff matrix X (J\times S); a portfolio h pays hX. The payoff space = all payoffs attainable by trading = the row space of X (a linear space). A security is redundant if its payoff can be replicated by the others. Example: x_A=(2,1),\ x_B=(1,1),\ x_C=(2,2.5)=3x_B-0.5x_A.

A contingent claim (Arrow–Debreu security) pays 1 in state s only. Every asset is a combination of contingent claims: x=(u,v)=u\cdot c(s_1)+v\cdot c(s_2).

Theorem: a market is complete (every payoff can be replicated) ⟺ \mathrm{rank}(X)=S.

Example: with \mathrm{rank}=2 two states are complete; with only one security x=(3,0), \mathrm{rank}=1 and consumption in state 2 cannot be provided — risks cannot be shared or hedged.

12.2 The SDF and risk sharing in complete markets

With completeness, the state price p(c(s)) prices any payoff x at \sum_sp(c(s))x(s); defining m(s)=p(c(s))/\pi(s) gives p(x)=E[mx]: the SDF exists. Risk sharing: the marginal rates of substitution between any two states are equal across individuals.

Example: Allen's future endowment is (2,0), Bob's (0,2), 1 each today, log utility, \beta=1, equally likely states. The Euler equations and market clearing give state prices of 1/2 each; in equilibrium h^A=(-1,1), h^B=(1,-1) and both consume (1,1): each sells the state claim he does not want in exchange for riskless consumption — both better off than without trade.

12.3 Risk-neutral probabilities

The riskless bond has R_f=1/\sum_sp(c(s)). Let

\pi^*(s)=\frac{p(c(s))}{\sum_{s'}p(c(s'))}=\pi(s)\frac{m(s)}{E[m]}.

\pi^*\in[0,1] sums to 1 and is a new probability measure. Then

p(x)=\frac{E^*[x]}{R_f}.

The price is the expected payoff under risk-neutral probabilities discounted at the riskless rate. The world described by \pi^* is populated by risk-neutral investors, so all assets earn the riskless return. Example: representative consumer with endowment (2,3), 1 today, u=-e^{-x}, \beta=1, equal odds: state prices e^{-1}/2\approx0.18, e^{-2}/2\approx0.07; \pi^*=(0.73,0.27); R_f=3.97; an asset paying (2,1) costs 0.44 (the same by state prices or by risk-neutral probabilities).

12.4 The law of one price

What about incomplete markets? The law of one price (LOOP): if hX=h'X then ph=ph'.

Proposition: LOOP ⟺ the pricing function q is linear ⟺ there is a unique m=z^* in the payoff space with p(x)=E[mx].

So neither complete markets nor an equilibrium model are needed — LOOP alone guarantees an SDF. With incomplete markets there are many SDFs outside the payoff space (m'=m+\varepsilon, E[\varepsilon x]=0); m is their projection onto the payoff space.

12.5 No arbitrage

An arbitrage is a portfolio h with hX\ge0,\ ph\le0 and at least one strict inequality. It includes: zero cost with a possibly positive payoff (a free lottery ticket), or negative cost (being paid to take a lottery ticket — a strong arbitrage). Do not mistake arbitrage for "riskless profit at zero cost" — that is only strong arbitrage.

Proposition: no arbitrage ⟹ LOOP; no arbitrage ⟺ there exists a strictly positive SDF.

So: the law of one price ⟺ an SDF exists; no arbitrage ⟺ an SDF exists and is positive.

12.6 Violations of the law of one price and limits to arbitrage

There are real violations: closed-end country funds at a premium (the Taiwan Fund at a 207% premium in early 1987, because US investors could not invest directly in Taiwan); ADR premia (Infosys's ADR at a 136% premium); Royal Dutch Shell: under the 1907 merger agreement cash flows are split 60:40, so the market-value ratio should be 1.5 but deviated for long stretches (Shell was not in the S&P 500 and index funds preferred Royal Dutch); dual-class stock (Molex); corporate spin-offs: 3Com's carve-out of Palm, Palm at 95 and 3Com at 82, implying a negative value for 3Com's remaining business (82-95\times1.525=-63 per share).

Why didn't arbitrageurs remove them? Limits to arbitrage: short-sale constraints (148% of Palm's floating shares were borrowed), institutional constraints (foreign-investment limits) and above all risk — violations of LOOP rarely create riskless arbitrage, just risky bets with good odds, especially with no certain terminal date, and spreads can widen before they narrow. LTCM had a $2.3 billion pairs trade on Royal Dutch/Shell, and when the spread widened in 1998 it was in distress.

13. Options

Intuition. An option is a choice: you exercise only when it helps, so its price is always positive. Its value can be fixed by replication and no arbitrage, independently of anyone's risk preferences.

13.1 Basics

A call is the right to buy the underlying at the strike X, a put the right to sell; the buyer (long side) pays the premium, the seller (short side, the writer) receives it; European options can be exercised only at expiry, American ones any time until then. At expiry a call pays \max(S-X,0) and a put \max(X-S,0); profit = payoff − premium. Example: a Google call with strike 250 and premium 4, with the stock at 270 at expiry: payoff 20, profit 16. In/at/out of the money: immediate exercise would give a positive/zero/negative payoff.

Options do not involve the company itself — they are side bets on the stock price. (A warrant is issued by the company, creates new shares on exercise and dilutes; employee options are similar.) Options trade on exchanges in standardised form and over the counter in customised form; the purposes are speculation and hedging.

13.2 Option strategies

A straddle (buy a call and a put at the same strike) bets on volatility; a bull spread (buy a low-strike call, sell a high-strike call) bets on a moderate rise; a protective put (stock + put) is portfolio insurance; a covered call (own the stock and write a call) is a conservative strategy; naked positions have no underlying. LTCM sold many straddles betting volatility would drop; it rose.

13.3 Put–call parity

A protective put (a European put + the stock) pays \max(X-S,0)+S=\max(X,S) at expiry; a call + a zero-coupon bond with face value X pays \max(S-X,0)+X=\max(S,X). Same payoffs, so the same price:

C+PV(X)=P+S.

With a dividend D paid just before expiry: C+PV(X)+PV(D)=P+S. Example: a one-year European call at 8, put at 2, strike 40, interest rate 10%: S=C-P+PV(X)=8-2+40/1.1=42.36. Implication: if you can price a call you can price a put; a covered call ≡ selling a put and buying a zero-coupon bond.

13.4 Early exercise and value bounds

Without dividends, an American call should never be exercised early: C^{AM}\ge C^{EU}>S-PV(X)>S-X, and exercising gives S-X, which is less than the option's value. So American call = European call. With dividends early exercise may be optimal; an American put may be optimal to exercise early (a firm in distress with a near-worthless stock: little more to gain by waiting and money has time value), so an American put is worth more than a European one. Bounds: S-PV(X)<C\le S (no dividends), i.e. \max(S-PV(X),0)\le C\le S.

Determinants of value (call/put): a higher strike lowers the call and raises the put; a higher stock price raises the call and lowers the put; higher volatility raises both; longer maturity raises American options; a higher interest rate raises the call and lowers the put.

13.5 The binomial (CRR) model and replication

Two dates. Example: stock 50, next year 60 or 40, interest 10%; value a call with strike 50. Replicate: buy x shares and borrow y so payoffs match: 60x-1.1y=10, 40x-1.1y=0 ⟹ x=1/2, y=18.18; cost 25-18.18=6.82 — the call's price. If the call traded at 10, sell it and buy the replicating portfolio for a zero payoff and a 3.18 gain today — arbitrage.

General binomial model: S moves to uS with probability p or dS with 1-p, the riskless gross return is R, and u>R>d is required (else arbitrage).

C=\frac1R\big[qC_u+(1-q)C_d\big],\qquad q=\frac{R-d}{u-d}\in(0,1).

q is the risk-neutral probability: under q the stock's expected return is qu+(1-q)d=R. The option price does not use the natural probability p — which does not mean it is independent of natural probabilities: they are embedded in u,d,R (or q).

Link to the SDF: take the representative-consumer economy e_0=1, e_1=(1,2), log utility, \beta=1, equal odds. m=e_0/e_1=(1,1/2), state prices (1/2,1/4), R=4/3; for a stock x_A=(1,4): p_A=3/2, u=8/3, d=2/3, q=(R-d)/(u-d)=1/3=\pi^*(s_2); a call with strike 2 has p=0\cdot\tfrac12+2\cdot\tfrac14=\tfrac12, the same as the binomial price. If the natural probabilities change to (2/3,1/3) then R'=6/5, p_A'=4/3, u'=3,\ d'=3/4, q'=1/5, C'=1/3 — it changes. An absolute pricing model (equilibrium) produces all prices, including u,d,R, endogenously; a relative pricing model (binomial) takes the stock and bond prices as given and prices only derivatives — which is why relative models are more successful (absolute models face the equity premium puzzle).

Multiple periods: the same u,d each period. Example: a 2-month European put, strike 63, monthly gross rate R=1.008, u=1.06,d=0.94, current price 62: q=0.567, leaves P_{uu}=0,P_{ud}=1.22,P_{dd}=8.22, P_u=0.52,\ P_d=4.22, P^E=2.11; the American put at the down node has early-exercise value 63-58.28=4.72>4.22, so P^A=2.32.

Matching the tree to data: use the mean \nu and volatility \sigma of geometric Brownian motion with u=1/d=e^{\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}}: daily (\Delta t=1/256) with \sigma=0.5 gives u=1.0317 and d=0.9692. Example: a heating-oil distributor: spot 2, on 1 December either 2.74 or 1.46, R=1.02, u=1.37, d=0.73, q=0.45. A customer pays 1 million up front for the right to buy 6 million gallons at 2.10 — a call; per gallon C=0.45\times0.64/1.02=0.2824, total 1.69 million >1 million: not a fair deal.

13.6 Black–Scholes

Let the binomial time step go to zero: the stock follows geometric Brownian motion dS/S=\nu\,dt+\sigma\,dZ (Z a Wiener process: dZ has mean 0 and variance dt, independent normal increments):

C=S\,N(d_1)-Xe^{-rT}N(d_2),\quad d_1=\frac{\ln(S/X)+(r+\sigma^2/2)T}{\sigma\sqrt T},\ d_2=d_1-\sigma\sqrt T.

Example: S=100,\ X=95,\ r=10\%,\ T=0.25,\ \sigma=0.5: C=13.70.

Real options: options embedded in investments (abandon, defer, expand) — a film studio making movies, deciding whether to quit.

14. Forwards, Futures and Swaps

Intuition. A forward locks in a future trading price at zero cost; its price is fixed by no arbitrage — the cost of carry — and not by anyone's expectation of the future price.

14.1 Forward contracts

A forward is an agreement to buy (long) or sell (short) an asset at a future date at an agreed price. Spot price S_t; forward price F_{t,T}: the price agreed at t for delivery at T. At inception the contract has zero value (unlike options, no premium is paid); the long's payoff at maturity is S_T-F_{0,T}.

The forward price = the future value of the spot price (no storage costs, no frictions, borrowing and lending at the same rate):

F_{t,T}=S_t(1+r)^{T-t}.

Proof: if F>S(1+r)^{T-t}, borrow S_t, buy the asset and short a forward: zero cost and a riskless payoff F-S_t(1+r)^{T-t}>0 — arbitrage. The other direction is similar. As t\to T, F_{t,T}\to S_T. Example: copper at 84.85 cents/lb, a 9-month T-bill priced at 970.89 (face 1000): 1+r=1.03, F=87.4 cents.

Storage costs and convenience yield: with storage cost c(t) at the end of each period, F_{0,T}=S_0(1+r)^T+\sum c(t)(1+r)^{T-t}. A known income stream (coupons, dividends) is negative storage cost: for a semi-annual 8% coupon bond with face 100, price 92.6 and annual rate 9%, the one-year forward price is 92.6\times1.045^2-4\times1.045-4=92.94. The convenience yield y (the benefit of holding the commodity) makes F_{0,T}\le cost of carry — owning the physical good is sometimes more convenient than holding a forward (a baker will not sell wheat inventory): F_{0,T}=(S_0+U_0)e^{(r-y)T} (U_0 the present value of storage costs). The higher the convenience yield the lower the forward price, which explains spot prices above forward prices.

The value of a forward after inception (t>0):

f_{0,t}=\frac{F_{t,T}-F_{0,T}}{(1+r)^{T-t}}=S_t-\frac{F_{0,T}}{(1+r)^{T-t}}.

With continuous compounding f_{0,t}=S_t-F_{0,T}e^{-r(T-t)}. Example: a long forward on a non-dividend stock with delivery price 24, spot 25, six months left, r=10\% continuous: f=25-24e^{-0.05}=2.17.

14.2 Futures

A futures contract is a standardised forward traded on an exchange, with a clearinghouse as counterparty, daily marking to market, a margin (typically 5%–10%) and a maintenance margin below which a call for more margin is made. Example: a baker buys 5000 bushels of wheat futures at 5.1, margin 10% (2550); gains and losses are settled daily and the futures price converges to the spot price at maturity.

Futures price = forward price (with deterministic rates): go long 1/(1+r)^{T-1} units, then raise the position each period to (1+r)^{-(T-t-1)} units, reinvesting all gains and losses at r, to collect S_T-F_{0,T} at maturity; adding a riskless investment of F_{0,T}/(1+r)^T yields exactly S_T. The same construction with a forward price G_{0,T} also yields S_T, so costs must be equal ⟹ G=F. The difference is marking to market (reducing default risk), which matters especially when the interest rate is positively correlated with the underlying's price. Stock-index futures (CSI 300: 300 yuan per point).

14.3 Hedging with derivatives

Long hedge: a food maker must buy 500,000 bushels of soybeans in six months; futures 0.33, spot 0.32; buy 100 contracts (5000 each): if the spot is 0.40 at expiry the futures gain (0.4-0.33)\times500000=35000 and the effective cost is 0.4-0.07=0.33 per bushel, a total of 165,000 — the price is locked in. Short hedge: a Chinese electronics firm will receive USD 500,000 in three months and fears yuan appreciation; it shorts 4 USD futures (125,000 USD each, 6.8 yuan/USD): at 6.5 the futures gain (850000-812500)\times4=150000, plus conversion 3250000, total 3400000=6.8 per dollar — the exchange rate is locked in.

Leverage and risk in futures: a bond futures price of 99 with margin 9.9: a price rise of 1 earns 1/9.9=10.1\% (buying the bond outright earns 1/98=1.02\%), and the same in the other direction as -10.1\%, with margin calls. Cases: Barings Bank collapsed in 1995 after losing $1.4 billion on Nikkei futures; Showa Shell lost $1.5 billion on currency futures; Metallgesellschaft lost over $1 billion on oil futures; JPMorgan lost at least $2 billion on CDS in 2012. Airlines hedging fuel: with futures, a price fall triggers margin calls (at the end of 2008 Delta and United each had about $1 billion of cash tied up as collateral). Options instead of futures: buy a call with strike 6 for $200,000: at 7 the net profit is \$800,000, at 4 the loss only $200,000 (futures: $1 million / −$2 million). A sovereign example: the Mexican government buys puts with strike $80 to set a price floor on Pemex's oil income — a protective put.

Principles of corporate risk management: identify the risks you are most uncomfortable with and not rewarded for; choose the appropriate instrument; avoid speculating with derivatives; take care with futures and forwards — make sure risk is hedged and not increased.

14.4 Swaps

An interest-rate swap exchanges two cash-flow streams, typically fixed against floating. Example: a bank holds a 5-year $1 million floating-rate (LIBOR) loan and swaps it for a fixed 6% with a dealer: year 1 LIBOR 5%, the bank receives 60,000 and pays 50,000, net +10,000; year 2 LIBOR 8%, the bank pays a net 20,000. Value zero at inception; positive or negative as rates move. A currency swap: AM Company needs EUR 11 million but issues $10 million 6% five-year notes in the US and swaps with a European bank, equivalent to a 5% euro loan. A credit default swap (CDS): the buyer pays a periodic spread and, on default, exchanges the defaulted loan for its face value; the buyer need not own the loan (a naked CDS) — a bet on creditworthiness. Example: a $10 million two-year CDS at a 5% spread: default after one year, the buyer paid 500,000 and receives $10 million. In the 2007–2008 crisis Wall Street created collateralised debt obligations (CDOs) depending on the performance of subprime mortgage pools; rating agencies badly underestimated their risk; investors who foresaw the collapse shorted subprime via CDS; AIG sold huge amounts of CDS protection without hedging, with exposure over $100 billion, and was bailed out.

15. Corporate Debt and the Option View

Intuition. Shareholders and creditors hold two option-like claims on the firm's assets: creditors take the capped part, shareholders the part above the cap.

15.1 Merton's model

A firm lives one period, owes creditors D at the end and has liquidation value V. Creditors get \min(V,D) and shareholders \max(V-D,0) — shareholders hold a call on the firm's assets with strike D, limited liability being the "right to walk away"; creditors own the firm and have written that call (Merton 1974).

By put–call parity: creditors hold a riskless discount bond with face value D and have written a put on the firm with strike D.

\text{value of risky debt}=\text{value of riskless debt}-\text{value of the put}.

Example: assets worth 10 today and 15 or 9 tomorrow (equally likely), promised repayment 13.35, interest rate 10%. Riskless debt is worth 13.35/1.1=12.14; the put pays 0 in the good state and 13.35-9=4.35 in the bad state; replicate by shorting 0.725 units of the asset and lending 9.89, worth 10\times(-0.725)+9.89=2.64; risky debt is 12.14-2.64=9.5 and equity 10-9.5=0.5.

A government loan guarantee: if the firm defaults the government makes up the difference, so creditors hold something equivalent to a riskless bond: the value of the guarantee = the value of the put = 2.64; after the guarantee debt is worth 12.14, equity is still 0.5 and the firm is worth 12.64, up by 2.64 — the guarantee benefits creditors and raises firm value.

15.2 Credit ratings and default prediction

Three major agencies: Moody's, S&P and Fitch; investment grade (Aaa/AAA to Baa/BBB), high-yield/junk (Ba/BB and below). Default probability is predicted by logit regression: with p the default probability, y=\ln\dfrac p{1-p} is linear in characteristics: y=a+b_1\,ROA+b_2\,\dfrac{\text{liabilities}}{\text{assets}}+b_3\,\dfrac{EBITDA}{\text{liabilities}}; higher ROA means fewer defaults, higher leverage more defaults, stronger debt-paying ability fewer defaults, and p=e^y/(1+e^y) gives the predicted probability.

16. Capital Structure

Intuition. Firm value is one pizza — financing with debt or equity is just how it is sliced. The MM theorem says that under ideal conditions the slicing does not change the size of the pizza. In reality taxes, bankruptcy costs and information problems change the answer.

16.1 MM Proposition I (no taxes)

Capital structure is the right-hand side of the balance sheet: V=D+E. Proposition I: V_L=V_U — capital structure does not affect firm value or the price per share.

Example: Firm A is all-equity with earnings 9 or 15 (equally likely), expected 12, cost of capital r_0=20\%, value 12/1.2=10; Firm B has the same business but debt of 5 (10%, riskless): bonds pay (5.5,5.5), stock (3.5,9.5), V_B=10. No-arbitrage proof: if B's stock were worth 6 (total 11>10), buy 5.5 of B's stock while borrowing 2.5, replicating A's shareholder payoffs (2.2,5.5)>(1.75,4.75) at the same cost — arbitrage. Homemade leverage: investors can replicate a firm's leverage by borrowing personally; corporate leverage does not affect the price. The case with default also works: Firm C promises 13.35, debt is worth 9.5 and stock 0.5, total still 10.

Assumptions: symmetric information; individuals and firms borrow at the same rate; no taxes; no arbitrage; no bankruptcy costs.

General case (perpetuities): constant EBIT in perpetuity, V=EBIT/r_{WACC}. Homemade-leverage proof: A has debt D_A, B has none, same earnings. If V_A>V_B: sell A's stock and buy B's with extra borrowing WD_A/E_A, earning \tfrac{W}{E_A}\tfrac{V_A}{V_B}(C-rD_A)>\tfrac W{E_A}(C-rD_A); if V_A<V_B similarly. So V_A=V_B.

16.2 The weighted average cost of capital and Proposition II

The cost of capital is the expected return on all the firm's securities = the opportunity cost of investing in the firm's assets.

r_{WACC}=r_e\frac EV+r_d\frac DV.

Proposition I is equivalent to r_{WACC}=r_0 (independent of leverage). Why can't a firm lower r_{WACC} by issuing debt? Debt is cheaper (r_d<r_e), but leverage makes equity riskier, raising r_e (and even r_d); the two effects exactly cancel:

Proposition II (no taxes): r_e=r_0+\dfrac DE(r_0-r_d) — the cost of equity rises linearly with leverage.

Proof: r_e=(EBIT-r_dD)/E and EBIT=r_0(D+E). In terms of \beta (CAPM holds): \beta_0=\beta_{WACC}=\beta_E\frac EV+\beta_D\frac DV; with riskless debt \beta_E=(1+D/E)\beta_0.

Example: Lobster Co. is all-equity with r_0=10\% and becomes levered with D/E=1/2, equity \beta=1.8, market premium 7.5%, r_f=1\%: \beta_0=1.2 (two ways: r_0=r_f+\beta_0\cdot7.5\%, or 1.8=1.5\beta_0); r_e=1\%+1.8\times7.5\%=14.5\% (or 10\%+\tfrac12(10\%-1\%)); r_{WACC}=\tfrac13\times1\%+\tfrac23\times14.5\%=10\%=r_0.

Example (financing a project): General Machines is all-equity with earnings of 10 million a year forever, r_0=10\%, 10 million shares, and will build a plant for 4 million adding 1 million a year. NPV =-4+1/0.1=6 (million). On announcement the value rises to 106 million, price 10.6. With equity financing: issue 4/10.6 million shares; with debt (6%): shareholders earn 10+1-0.24=10.76, r_e=10.76/106=10.15\%=10\%+(10\%-6\%)\cdot4/106 — consistent with Proposition II; firm value is 110 million either way — consistent with Proposition I.

16.3 With corporate taxes

Interest is deductible: the tax shield t_cr_dD is a perpetuity with the same risk as the debt, present value t_cD:

V_L=V_U+t_cD,\qquad V_U=\frac{EBIT(1-t_c)}{r_0}.

Example: EBIT 1 million; no debt versus debt of 4 million at 10%, tax 35%: no debt, after-tax 650,000; with debt (interest 400,000) after tax 390,000, which together with interest gives investors 790,000 — the extra 140,000 is the tax shield t_cr_dD.

Proposition II (with taxes): r_e=r_0+(r_0-r_d)(1-t_c)\dfrac DE — rising more slowly. WACC: r_{WACC}=r_0\Big(1-t_c\dfrac DV\Big) falls with leverage. \beta_E=[1+(1-t_c)D/E]\beta_0 (riskless debt). Example (Divided Airlines): r_0=20\%, value 500, 100 shares; borrow 200 and repurchase shares, t_c=35\%, r_d=5\%: V_L=500+0.35\times200=570; on announcement the price rises to 5.7 and the firm buys back 200/5.7=35 shares, leaving 65, equity 570-200=370, per share 370/65=5.7 (leverage raised the share price); r_e=0.2+(0.2-0.05)(0.65)(200/370)=25.27\%; r_{WACC}=0.2527\times\tfrac{370}{570}+0.05\times\tfrac{200}{570}\times0.65=17.54\%<20\%.

16.4 The trade-off theory

With only the tax shield the optimum would be 100% debt — which is not what we see. Debt cannot rise without limit: bankruptcy has costs (legal and administrative fees, direct costs) and financial-distress costs (losing customers and suppliers, depreciating intangibles, indirect costs). The MM propositions require costless bankruptcy; with costs creditors must first pay lawyers: Firm C's debt is worth <9.5.

V_L=V_U+t_cD-f(D), with f rising ever faster in debt (convex).

Example: f(D)=aD^2+b, first-order condition t_c-2aD^*=0 ⟹ D^*=t_c/(2a). The trade-off: the benefit of the tax shield against the cost of financial distress; r_{WACC} first falls then rises, lowest at D^*. Value decomposition: V=E+D+T+F (E+D are tradable claims, T taxes, F distress costs, T+F non-tradable).

Predictions: firms with a high share of tangible assets (real estate, airlines) borrow more — low distress costs; firms with uncertain earnings (high-tech) borrow less; more profitable firms have higher target leverage (the last is not supported empirically).

16.5 The pecking-order theory

Asymmetric information: managers know more than investors. Issuing stock may signal that management thinks the stock is overvalued; internal financing or debt signals confidence in the new project. So financing follows an order: first internal funds (retained earnings), then new debt, and only last new equity. Implications: more profitable firms borrow less (because they have enough internal funds, not because of a low target ratio); firms whose investment opportunities outrun internal funds borrow more and more; there is no well-defined target debt ratio.

16.6 Evidence

In a survey of 392 CFOs, 81% use target debt ratios (consistent with the trade-off theory); most firms have low debt ratios and some use none; industries differ markedly (2005: air transport 59.67%, building construction 40.39%, hotels 57.78%; drugs 5.81%, software 2.27%, computers 3.77%). Rajan and Zingales (1995): debt ratios depend on size (larger firms higher), tangible assets (higher), profitability (lower) and market-to-book (growth firms lower) — points 2 and 4 support the trade-off theory, points 1, 3 and 4 the pecking order. No single theory explains everything: the pecking order works best for large firms with access to public bond markets, while small young growth firms rely more on equity.
